content.text: Purpose To build real partnerships between the school, families, students, and community stakeholders. These partnerships respect local culture. They support student learning, wellbeing, and whole-person development, in line with Eduversal's mission and Schoolwide Learner Outcomes (SLOs).

Eduversal Partner Schools see parents and guardians as essential partners in the learning journey. They are not passive receivers of educational services. Our approach to family and community engagement is based on Joyce Epstein's Framework of Six Types of Involvement. The six types are parenting, communicating, volunteering, learning at home, decision-making, and collaborating with community. This framework gives a full model for building real partnerships.

This approach has deep roots in Indonesian cultural values, especially the principle of gotong royong (mutual cooperation). Gotong royong stresses shared responsibility and community support. In Indonesian society, education is traditionally a shared effort between family, school, and community. Deep respect for elders and for shared wisdom guides children's development.

For Islamic schools in the Eduversal network, Islamic principles make this partnership even stronger. These principles stress the sacred duty (fardhu kifayah) of educating children, and the hadith teaching that "each of you is a shepherd and each of you is responsible for his flock." Parents, teachers, and community members together form the support that students need to grow both academically and spiritually.

At the center of our approach is a firm commitment to equity. We value and welcome all families, whatever their social and economic status, educational background, or language level. We know that engagement may look different from one family to another. We actively work to remove barriers to taking part, so that every voice is heard and respected.
content.title: 16.1.1 Philosophy of Partnership

content.text: These principles guide all engagement work at Eduversal Partner Schools:
content.title: 16.1.2 Core Principles

steps: Transparency: Open, honest, and timely communication builds trust. Schools share school policies, decisions, and student progress information with families without waiting to be asked.
Accessibility: Information is in plain language and in both English and Bahasa Indonesia. We recognize that families speak different languages, and we provide translation support when needed.

Inclusivity: We actively involve families from different backgrounds. This includes English as an Additional Language (EAL) learners and students with Special Educational Needs (SEN). It also includes families of different social and economic backgrounds and families with limited access to technology. (See Section 8: Inclusion, EAL, and Learning Support for extra guidance.)
Mutual Respect: We value the knowledge, cultural views, and life experience that families bring. We build respect for culture into all communication and engagement strategies.

Collaborative Decision-Making: The Yayasan (Foundation) and school leadership keep governance authority. Even so, we actively ask stakeholders for input on matters that affect the school community. Parent and student views help shape school improvement priorities. (See Section 1: Front Matter and Governance Charter for governance structure.)
Responsiveness: We listen actively to feedback. We quickly let people know we have received their concerns. We close the loop by telling people how we have dealt with or used their input.

content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools work in a rich Indonesian cultural setting. This setting shapes how schools engage families:
content.title: 16.1.3 Indonesian Context Considerations

steps: Extended Family Structures: Grandparents, aunts, uncles, and other relatives often take part in decisions. Schools should be ready to work with several family members and respect their input on student matters.

Religious Considerations: Islamic schools must plan school schedules and parent events around prayer times, Ramadan schedules, and Friday Jumu'ah prayers. This also applies to Islamic holidays (Eid al-Fitr, Eid al-Adha, Maulid Nabi). For non-Muslim families in Eduversal schools, schools must recognize and respect Christian holidays (Christmas, Easter), Hindu celebrations (Nyepi, Galungan), and Buddhist observances.

Communication Preferences: WhatsApp is the main communication platform in Indonesia. It often reaches parents better than email. However, official records should still be kept through email and school systems. Home visits (kunjungan rumah) are a normal part of the culture. Families value them deeply as a sign of care and commitment.

Parental Work Patterns: Many parents work shifts, travel often for business, or run family businesses with long hours. Evening and weekend activities and flexible ways to communicate keep these families connected to their children's education.

content.text: The table below shows the main communication channels that Eduversal Partner Schools use. It keeps communication consistent and clear across the network:
Response Time Expectations: To build trust and give timely support, these response time standards apply:
content.title: 16.2.1 Official Communication Channels

steps: Email inquiries: Within 48 hours (2 business days)
Urgent concerns (safeguarding, medical emergencies): Immediate response (within 2 hours during school hours)
Non-urgent requests: Within 5 business days

content.text: Professional Communication Guidelines: All staff members must follow these standards:

steps: Use only school-approved platforms for parent communication. Staff must not use personal social media accounts (e.g., personal Facebook, Instagram) for parent-teacher communication. (See Section 12: Staff Code of Conduct for social media guidelines.)
Keep a professional tone and professional boundaries in all communications. Avoid language that is too casual and replies driven by strong emotion.
Protect confidentiality: Never discuss other students or families in communications with parents.
Escalation pathway: If a concern cannot be solved at teacher level, it should be escalated in this order:
Teacher → Subject Leader/Coordinator → Principal → Foundation Representative (General Manager)

content.text: Bilingual Communication Standards: Eduversal Partner Schools serve communities that speak different languages. To make sure all families can access information:
content.title: 16.2.3 Language and Accessibility Policy

steps: All school-wide communications (newsletters, policy announcements, event invitations): In English, with a Bahasa Indonesia summary or a full translation.
Parent-facing forms (consent forms, enrollment documents, field trip permissions): Full versions are available in both languages.

Report cards: Written in English to match Cambridge standards. Explanatory notes and key terms are translated into Bahasa Indonesia. (See Section 6: Assessment, Reporting, and Data Use for reporting formats.)
Emergency communications: SMS/WhatsApp alerts in both languages at the same time, so that everyone understands immediately.

content.text: Plain Language Guidelines: Educational terms can confuse families. To make communication clear:

steps: Avoid jargon where possible. When a technical term is necessary, give a clear definition.
Example: Instead of "formative assessment," write "ongoing check-ins to track learning progress and adjust teaching."
Provide a Cambridge Terminology Glossary for Parents (see Appendix 16A). It explains terms like IGCSE, AS Level, A Level, Checkpoint, coursework, and moderation.

content.text: Accommodations for Diverse Families:

steps: Translation services: Available for Parent-Teacher Conferences on request (48-hour advance notice required). Work with school admin to arrange interpreters.
Visual aids: Use infographics and visual schedules for complex information such as exam timetables, curriculum overviews, and school procedures.

Digital accessibility: The school website targets WCAG (Web Content Accessibility Guidelines) 2.2 Level AA. This is the network accessibility benchmark in Website Minimum Standards 26-27. It makes the website accessible for families with visual impairments or other disabilities.

content.text: In emergencies or crises (natural disasters, security incidents, health outbreaks), clear and fast communication is essential. Emergency Communication Protocol:
content.title: 16.2.4 Emergency and Crisis Communications

steps: Immediate notification: An SMS/WhatsApp alert to all parents within 30 minutes of an incident, with the essential information (e.g., "School is in lockdown. All students are safe. More information to follow.").
Follow-up communication: A detailed email or letter from the Principal within 24 hours. It explains the situation, the actions taken, and the next steps.
Ongoing updates: Updates every 4-6 hours until the situation is resolved or stabilized.
Designated spokesperson: The Principal or Foundation Representative is the official spokesperson for media questions. Staff should send all media questions to the Principal.

content.text: Emergency Communication Tree: For detailed emergency response procedures, see Section 15: Risk Management, Emergency Preparedness, and Business Continuity. The emergency communication tree makes sure information spreads quickly:

steps: Principal → Assistant Principals/Coordinators → Homeroom Teachers → Parents
Foundation Representative → Yayasan Board
Principal → Local authorities (if required)

content.title: Official communication channels
rows: Official notices, individual student communications, formal documentation
Grades, assignments, attendance records, curriculum updates
Quick updates, daily reminders, informal communications
Policies, annual calendar, news articles, event information
School highlights, upcoming events, student achievements, community spotlight

content.text: Consistent, predictable communication builds trust and keeps families informed. Eduversal Partner Schools set regular communication rhythms across the school year.
Class Newsletters (Homeroom Teachers): Each week, homeroom teachers send families a one-page update by email and WhatsApp. It includes:
content.title: 16.3.1 Weekly Communications

steps: This Week's Learning Highlights: A short summary of key topics in Math, English, Science, and other subjects.
Upcoming Assessments: Reminders of quizzes, projects, or unit tests planned for the next week.
Homework Reminders: Clear outline of homework expectations and due dates.
Character Spotlight: Recognition of a student who showed an SLO (e.g., Ethical Leadership, Global Competence) or a Profil Pelajar Pancasila attribute.
Next Week's Focus: Preview of upcoming learning goals.

content.text: Example: "This week in Grade 5, students explored ecosystems in Science and practiced persuasive writing in English. Next week, we'll begin our unit on fractions and host a guest speaker on conservation. Homework: Reading log due Friday. Character Spotlight: Congratulations to Aisyah for demonstrating compassion by helping a new classmate settle in!"
Principal's Newsletter: Each month, the Principal publishes a 2-3 page newsletter. It goes out by email and is posted on the school website. It includes:
content.title: 16.3.2 Monthly Communications

steps: School Updates: Important announcements, policy changes, and new initiatives.
Event Recaps: Highlights and photos from recent events (Sports Day, Cultural Festival, charity drives).
Student Achievements: Celebration of academic, sports, arts, and character achievements (Cambridge exam successes, olympiad awards, community service milestones).
Community Spotlight: A feature on a parent volunteer, staff member, or community partner who is making a difference.
Calendar of Upcoming Events: Key dates for the next month, including public holidays, Parent Workshops, PTCs (parent-teacher conferences), and school events.

content.text: Progress Reports: (See Section 6.9: Report Cards and Progress Reports for detailed reporting formats.)

steps: Mid-term reports: Focus on effort, behavior, and progress toward learning goals. Written comments highlight strengths and areas for growth.
End-of-semester reports: Include academic grades, detailed written comments, and progress toward SLOs and Profil Pelajar Pancasila competencies.
content.title: 16.3.3 Semester Communications

content.text: Parent-Teacher Conference Invitations: Invitations go out two weeks before the planned PTC window. They use an online booking system where parents can:

steps: Select preferred time slots (in-person, virtual, or phone conference options).
Indicate need for translation support.
Submit specific questions or topics they wish to discuss.

content.text: School Calendar (Published in June for upcoming academic year): The annual calendar is a key planning tool for families. It includes:
content.title: 16.3.4 Annual Communications

steps: Academic term dates and semester breaks.
Indonesian public holidays (Independence Day, Eid celebrations, Christmas, Nyepi).
Assessment windows (Cambridge exam periods, EASE administration, internal examinations).
Key school events (Open House, Sports Day, Cultural Festival, Parent Education Workshops, College Fair).

content.text: Annual Report to Community (Published in July): At the end of each academic year, the Principal publishes an Annual Report. It summarizes:

steps: School Achievements: Cambridge examination results, university placements, olympiad successes, accreditation progress.
Data Summary: Enrollment trends, student demographics, staff qualifications, SLO attainment rates.
Financial Transparency: Budget overview, capital projects, and major spending (approved by Yayasan). (See Section 13: Operations, Finance, and Resources for financial protocols.)
Strategic Priorities: Goals and focus areas for the next school year, in line with the School Improvement Plan (SIP). (See Section 4.2.2 for the SIP development process.)

content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools commit to giving parents the knowledge and skills to support their children's learning and wellbeing at home.

Annual Workshop Calendar: Schools offer at least four parent workshops each year on topics relevant to the Eduversal community. Workshops take place on weekday evenings or Saturday mornings so that working parents can attend.

Example Workshop Topics:

Understanding the Cambridge Curriculum (September):
content.title: 16.4.1 Parent Education Series

items: Overview of Cambridge Primary, Lower Secondary, IGCSE, AS, and A Level programs. Explanation of assessment formats, grading systems, and university recognition. Q&A session with Subject Leaders.

content.text: Supporting English as an Additional Language (EAL) Learners at Home (October):

items: Practical ways to build English skills at home, including reading routines, vocabulary games, and using online resources. Presented by the EAL Coordinator. (See Section 8.4 for the EAL support framework.)

content.text: Preparing for Cambridge Examinations (December):

items: Guidance on exam preparation, study techniques, managing stress, and understanding exam requirements. Includes sessions for IGCSE and A Level students. (See Section 10: Cambridge Examinations Management.)

content.text: Digital Citizenship and Online Safety (February):

items: Helps parents understand cyberbullying, screen time management, and social media risks. Also covers ways to monitor and guide children's online behavior. Led by the IT Coordinator and the Student Wellbeing Counselor.

content.text: Wellbeing and Mental Health for Teens (April):

items: Covers adolescent mental health, how to recognize signs of anxiety or depression, and how to support students through academic and social pressures. Guest speakers may include school counselors or external mental health professionals. (See Section 9.13.5 for student wellbeing programs.)

content.text: University Admissions and College Counseling (May):

items: For secondary students and families. It covers how to apply to university, scholarship opportunities, writing a personal statement, and how international university systems work. The College Counselor leads it. (See Section 23 for college counseling support.)

content.text: Workshop Logistics:

steps: Format: Interactive presentations (45-60 minutes), followed by Q&A. Sessions are given in two languages, or live translation is provided.
Attendance Tracking: Sign-in sheets are kept as evidence for accreditation and for evaluating the program.
Post-Event Feedback: Short surveys are sent out to check satisfaction and to collect ideas for future topics.
Materials: Handouts and slides are shared by email and posted on the Parent Portal for families who are not able to attend.

content.text: Every year, all families receive a Parent Handbook at the start of the school year (printed copy and digital PDF). The handbook includes:
content.title: 16.4.2 Parent Handbook

steps: School mission, vision, and Schoolwide Learner Outcomes (SLOs).
Academic calendar and daily schedule.
Policies: attendance, homework, uniform, behavior expectations, safeguarding. (See the relevant sections of this Principal's Handbook.)
How to communicate with the school, and contact details for key staff.
What the school expects from parents in taking part and volunteering.
Complaints and grievance procedures. (See Section 16.6 below.)

content.text: The school website has a Parent Resource Library. It has guides, articles and videos that parents can download, on topics such as:
content.title: 16.4.3 Resource Library for Parents

steps: Supporting literacy and numeracy at home.
Understanding Profil Pelajar Pancasila.
Understanding learning differences (special educational needs (SEN), dyslexia, ADHD).
Helping children build resilience and a growth mindset.
Understanding Cambridge subject choices and pathways.

content.text: When parents take an active part, the school community becomes richer and the home-school partnership becomes stronger.
Structure and Purpose: Each Eduversal Partner School has a Parent-Teacher Association (PTA). The PTA is an advisory body that:
content.title: 16.5.1 Parent-Teacher Association (PTA)

steps: Helps communication between families and school leaders.
Organizes events that bring the community together (e.g., Cultural Festival, Family Fun Day, charity fundraisers).
Supports school projects by coordinating volunteers and raising funds.
Gives school leaders feedback on policies and programs.

content.text:
Note: The PTA is advisory. It does not have governance authority. Governance decisions stay with the Yayasan and the Principal. (See Section 1: Front Matter and Governance Charter.)

PTA Elections and Membership:

steps: Elections take place every year in August for the key positions: Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson, Secretary, Treasurer.
All parents/guardians are PTA members automatically and can vote.
Term limits: A maximum of two terms in a row in each position, so that leadership changes over time.
Meetings take place monthly (or as needed). Minutes are written and shared with the Principal.

content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools welcome parent volunteers in different roles:
content.title: 16.5.2 Volunteer Opportunities

steps: Classroom Volunteers: Helping teachers with activities, reading groups, or art projects. (Background checks are required; see Section 9: Safeguarding for safer recruitment procedures.)
Event Support: Helping organize Sports Day, Cultural Festival, Open House, field trips, and charity events.
Library Assistants: Helping to run the library, organize books, and support reading programs.
Career Talks and Guest Speakers: Parents with expertise in a specific field (medicine, engineering, business, arts) are invited to share their knowledge with students.
Mentorship Programs: Former students (alumni) or parent volunteers mentor students on exploring careers, applying to university, or personal development.

content.text: Volunteer Coordination:

steps: A Parent Liaison Coordinator (a staff role) recruits, schedules and trains volunteers.
Volunteers fill in a simple application form. They also attend a short orientation on confidentiality, safeguarding and school expectations.
Volunteer hours are recorded. Volunteers are recognized at an annual Volunteer Appreciation Event (June).

content.text: Micro-Volunteering: Not all families can commit to regular or long-term roles. So schools offer small volunteering tasks (micro-volunteering):

steps: Short, one-time tasks (e.g., baking food for a bake sale, translating a document, giving materials for a project).
Volunteering from home or online (e.g., checking draft letters and messages, doing practice interviews with students).

content.text: Home visits are a valued Indonesian tradition. They are a strong way to build relationships between teachers and families. Purpose:
content.title: 16.5.3 Home Visits (Kunjungan Rumah)

steps: Show care and commitment to the student's development as a whole person.
Understand the student's home, family relationships and cultural background.
Build trust and open communication.

content.text: Guidelines:

steps: Homeroom teachers visit the home of each student at least once per academic year, usually in Term 1 (September-October).
Visits are planned in advance with the parents' consent, at a time that suits both sides.
Teachers visit in pairs, for safety and professionalism.
Visits are informal conversations. They focus on getting to know the family and understanding the student's strengths, interests and challenges.
Teachers fill in a Home Visit Reflection Form (Appendix 16I). They record what they learned and use it to shape their teaching.

content.text: (See the Teacher Guidebook for detailed home visit procedures.)
Eduversal Partner Schools value feedback from parents, students and community members. They use this feedback to keep improving.
Purpose and Timing: Each May, all families are invited to fill in an anonymous Annual Parent Satisfaction Survey. It measures how satisfied they are with:
content.title: 16.6.1 Annual Parent Satisfaction Survey

steps: Communication effectiveness
Academic programs and teaching quality
Student support services (EAL, SEN, counseling)
Facilities and resources
Safeguarding and wellbeing
Opportunities for parent involvement

content.text: Survey Design:

steps: 20-25 questions: a mix of rating-scale (Likert) questions and open questions.
Bilingual (English and Bahasa Indonesia).
Sent by email, with reminders. Paper copies are available on request.

content.text: Data Analysis and Action Planning:

steps: The leadership team analyzes the results in June. It looks for trends, strengths and areas for improvement.
A summary of the findings is shared with staff, the PTA and the Yayasan.
Action steps are added to the School Improvement Plan (SIP) for the next year. (See Section 4.2.2 for how the SIP is developed.)
Key findings and planned actions are shared with families in the July newsletter and the August Parent Handbook.

content.text: Target Response Rate: At least 60% of families complete the survey. Ways to raise the response rate include:

steps: Explaining clearly what the survey is for and what difference it makes.
Multiple reminder emails.
Rewards (e.g., a prize draw for completed surveys).
Offering paper versions at school events.

content.text: Parents can give informal feedback at any time through:
content.title: 16.6.2 Informal Feedback Channels

steps: Parent Liaison Coordinator: A named staff member who receives and responds to parent questions, suggestions or concerns.
Principal's Open Office Hours: Set times (e.g., first Friday of each month, 8:00-10:00 AM). Parents can come in and speak with the Principal without an appointment.
Suggestion Box: A suggestion box in the school lobby and an online form on the school website.

content.text:
When an informal solution is not enough, parents may make a formal complaint. They follow the process below.

Step 1: Informal Resolution

Parents are encouraged to try to solve the matter informally first by:
content.title: 16.6.3 Formal Complaints Procedure

steps: Discussing the concern directly with the relevant teacher or Homeroom Teacher.
If the matter is not solved, taking it to the Subject Leader or Coordinator.

content.text:
Step 2: Formal Written Complaint

If the informal route does not solve the matter, parents may send a Formal Complaint Form (Appendix 16D) to the Principal. The form must include:

steps: Description of the issue or concern.
Steps already taken to resolve the matter.
Desired outcome or resolution.

content.text: Step 3: Investigation and Response

steps: The Principal confirms receipt within 2 business days.
The Principal investigates. This may include interviewing staff, reviewing records and checking policies.
A written response is given within 10 business days. It sets out the findings and the proposed solution.

content.text:
Step 4: Further Appeal

If the parent is not satisfied with the Principal's response, the complaint follows the network complaints ladder in Section 2.15. That section is the controlling text. First, the appeal goes to the General Manager. The General Manager decides within 10 working days, and this decision is final at school level. Then, serious or unresolved matters go to the local Yayasan Board and/or the Chief Academic Officer, who review them within 15 working days. Finally, they go to external authorities (Dinas Pendidikan, Ministry of Education, labor courts, or police) where the law provides for this.

Confidentiality and Non-Retaliation:

steps: All complaints are handled confidentially and professionally.
No retaliation against students or families who file complaints.
The Principal keeps a complaints log, as evidence for accreditation and to support continuous improvement.

content.text: (See the Teacher Guidebook for grievance policy details.)

content.title: Safeguarding complaints - carve-out
content.text: A complaint that raises a safeguarding or child-protection concern does NOT follow the parent complaints ladder in this section. It goes immediately to the Designated Safeguarding Lead (DSL) and is handled under Section 9. Under Permendikdasmen No. 6/2026 (BSAN), the Principal is the single accountable officer. Serious cases are escalated outside the school, to the Pokja BSAN at kabupaten/kota level. A safeguarding concern is never resolved by the school alone as an internal complaint. The parent complaints escalation route in Section 2.15 does not apply to it.

editorialNotes.text:
Step 4: Further Appeal

If the parent is dissatisfied with the Principal's response, the complaint follows the network complaints ladder in Section 2.15, which is the controlling text: appeal first to the General Manager (decision within 10 working days — final at school level), then, for serious or unresolved matters, to the local Yayasan Board and/or the Chief Academic Officer (review within 15 working days), and finally to external authorities (Dinas Pendidikan, Ministry of Education, labor courts, or police) where the law provides. (Aligned 2026-08-20: this step previously ended the procedure at the General Manager, whose decision was described as final after fifteen business days; the ladder in 2.15 continues past the GM.)

Confidentiality and Non-Retaliation:

content.text: Parent-Teacher Conferences are key meetings for one-to-one communication about the student's progress, goal-setting, and working together on learning.

steps: At least twice per year. For Grades 7–12, conferences take place in each semester, on dates each school sets on its Academic Calendar. They are normally held around the Mid-Term Progress Reports (October and March) and the end-of-semester reports (December and May). The Semester 1 and Semester 2 portfolio-led Student-Led Conferences normally fall in the December and May windows (see Section 6.10 and 16.8.4).
Parents or teachers may ask for extra conferences when needed.
content.title: 16.7.1 Frequency and Format

content.text: Conference Options:

steps: In-person: At school, in rooms set aside for conferences.
Virtual: By Zoom or Google Meet, for families who are not able to come in person.
Phone conference: An option for families with limited internet access.

content.text: Teacher Preparation: Teachers prepare for PTCs (parent-teacher conferences) by:
content.title: 16.7.2 Preparation and Scheduling

steps: Looking at student data (grades, attendance, behavior records, formative assessments).
Filling in a PTC Summary Form (Appendix 16C) with the main points to discuss: academic progress, social-emotional development, strengths, areas for growth, and individual goals.
Collecting samples of student work to show parents.

content.text: Parent Preparation: Two weeks before conferences, parents receive a PTC Preparation Form (Appendix 16B). The form encourages them to:

steps: Reflect on their child's strengths, challenges, and interests.
Prepare questions or topics they want to discuss.
Say which language they prefer and whether they need translation support.

content.text: Scheduling:

steps: An online booking system lets parents choose their preferred time slot (15-20 minutes per conference).
Translation is arranged for families who ask for support.

content.text: Good PTCs are structured, positive and focused on action. Key elements include:
content.title: 16.7.3 Conference Content

steps: Celebration of Strengths: Start with positive comments about the student's achievements, character, and contributions.
Academic Progress: Share data (grades, assessment results) and discuss progress toward curriculum expectations.
Social-Emotional Development: Talk about the student's wellbeing, relationships with classmates, and behavior.
Goal Setting: Together, set 2-3 specific, achievable goals for the student to work on before the next conference.
Home-School Partnership: Discuss ways parents can support learning and the goals at home.
Next Steps: Make the follow-up actions clear (e.g., extra support, monitoring progress, next check-in date).
Teachers record the key points from each conference on the PTC Summary Form (Appendix 16C).
Forms are kept in student records. They are reviewed at later conferences to track progress.
Attendance records are kept as evidence for accreditation.
content.title: 16.7.4 Documentation

content.text: Target Attendance Rate: At least 90% of families take part in PTCs. Families who are not able to attend are kept informed in another way (email summary, phone call).

editorialNotes.text: Corrected 2026-09-30: this step previously tied conferences to Term 1 and Term 2 report cards; the live Curriculum Module: Assessment Policy 26-27 schedules them by semester.

content.text: Helping students take an active part in shaping their school experience is central to Eduversal's commitment to the Ethical Leadership and Global Competence SLOs.
Purpose and Structure: Each Eduversal Partner School has a Student Council. It represents the students and gives input on school matters.
content.title: 16.8.1 Student Council

steps: Membership: Representatives are elected from each grade level (Grades 3-12).
Roles: President, Vice President, Secretary, and grade-level representatives.
Elections: Held every year in September through a democratic vote. Candidates give speeches and share campaign materials.

content.text: Responsibilities:

steps: Speak up for students' interests and concerns.
Plan and run student-led events (e.g., Spirit Week, Charity Drives, Talent Shows).
Give school leaders feedback on policies, programs, and school culture.
Serve as ambassadors at school events and Open House.

content.text: Meetings:

steps: Monthly meetings, run by a Student Council Advisor (a teacher role).
Meeting minutes are written and shared with the Principal and the student body.

content.text: Frequency and Purpose: Students complete anonymous voice surveys twice per year (November and May). The surveys ask what they think about:
content.title: 16.8.2 Student Voice Surveys

steps: Quality of teaching and learning.
School safety and wellbeing.
Inclusivity and respect for diversity.
Opportunities for leadership and voice.
Extracurricular and enrichment offerings.

content.text: Survey Design:

steps: Versions suited to the age of Primary (Grades 3-6) and Secondary (Grades 7-12) students.
Bilingual for EAL students.
A mix of rating-scale (Likert) questions and open questions.

content.text: Analysis and Action:

steps: Student Council Advisor and Principal analyze results.
Key findings are shared with the Student Council and staff.
Action is taken on student concerns (e.g., adding new clubs, improving cafeteria options, improving communication channels).
Students are told about changes made because of their feedback. This shows them that their voice matters.

content.text:
Purpose: As well as surveys, the Principal leads small student focus groups (6-8 students) once per term. The groups look more deeply at specific topics.

Format:
content.title: 16.8.3 Student Focus Groups

steps: Informal, conversational setting.
Topics may include: school culture, academic pressures, extracurricular interests, suggestions for improvement.
Notes are recorded and used to guide decisions.

content.text: For Grades 7–12, every Eduversal school runs Student-Led Conferences (SLCs) as part of the Student Learning layer. The student is the main presenter. The student uses selected portfolio evidence to explain their learning, challenges, progress and goals to parents. The teacher facilitates. There are two portfolio-led SLC cycles a year, one in each semester, on dates each school sets. They normally fall in the December and May final-report/parent-conference windows. Each conference takes about 15–20 minutes. The portfolio and the SLC are formative and not graded. The SLC does not automatically replace Parent-Teacher Conferences (Student Learning: Overview 26-27; Student Learning: Student-Led Conference 26-27). Early Years and Primary follow the Primary Director's separately issued documents. This approach:

steps: Lets students take charge of their own learning.
Develops communication and self-reflection skills.
Strengthens the student-parent-teacher partnership.
content.title: 16.8.4 Student-Led Conferences

content.text: Implementation Tips:

steps: Give students set templates to prepare their presentations (portfolio of work, self-assessment, goal-setting).
Run practice sessions to build confidence.

During the conference, the teacher guides but does not present. The teacher observes, takes short notes where useful, and prompts only when the student becomes stuck. Coaching happens before the conference, during preparation and practice.

content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools reach beyond the school walls through strategic partnerships with local and global organizations.

Philosophy: Service learning links meaningful community service with academic learning. It builds students' sense of civic responsibility, empathy, and global competence. All students take part in age-appropriate service learning projects each year.

Service Learning Cycle:
content.title: 16.9.1 Service Learning Program

steps: Identify a Need: Students research and identify a community need or social issue (e.g., environmental conservation, literacy support for underprivileged children, elderly care).
Plan Action: Students write a detailed project plan that sets out goals, activities, timeline, and required resources. (Use Appendix 16J: Service Learning Project Plan Template.)
Take Action: Students carry out the project (e.g., tree planting campaign, tutoring program, charity fundraiser, awareness campaign).
Reflect and Learn: Students reflect on their experience through journals, discussions, or presentations. They connect the service to academic learning and personal growth.
Celebrate and Share: Students share their impact with the school community through assemblies, newsletters, or social media.

content.text: Examples of Service Learning Projects:

steps: Primary students: Collecting books for a village library, creating care packages for orphanages.
Secondary students: Teaching English to community members, organizing environmental clean-up initiatives, fundraising for disaster relief.

content.text: Documentation:

steps: Each student's service learning hours are logged. They are checked against the graduation requirement in Section 2.16 (60 hours of community service over three years).
Project plans, photos, and student reflections are kept as evidence for accreditation and university applications.

content.text: (See the Teacher Guidebook for detailed service learning procedures.)
Partnership Development: Principals actively build relationships with local organizations, businesses, and NGOs that can support student learning and school operations. Examples include:
content.title: 16.9.2 Community Partnerships

steps: Local universities: Working together on STEAM projects, guest lectures, and dual enrollment opportunities.
Businesses: Sponsorships, internships, career talks, and mentorship programs.
NGOs: Joint service learning projects, expert speakers on global issues.
Cultural organizations: Field trips to museums, performances at the school, cultural exchange programs.

content.text: Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs): Make partnerships formal with signed MOUs (Appendix 16E). Each MOU sets out:

steps: Objectives and mutual benefits.
Roles and responsibilities of each party.
Length of the partnership and renewal terms.
Evaluation criteria (to check how well the partnership works annually).

content.text: Partnership Review: Partnerships are reviewed annually (March) to look at impact, challenges, and renewal. The findings are documented and shared with the Yayasan and the school community.

Purpose: Alumni are valuable ambassadors, mentors, and supporters of Eduversal schools. Strong alumni relations keep a lifelong connection with the school. They also give current students role models and career guidance.

Alumni Database:
content.title: 16.9.3 Alumni Relations

steps: Keep an up-to-date database of alumni contact details, career paths, and university placements.
The data is updated through annual surveys, social media outreach, and networking events.

content.text: Alumni Engagement Activities:

steps: Annual Reunions: Held every 2-3 years to bring alumni back to campus for networking and celebrations.
Career Talks: Alumni are invited to speak about their jobs, university experiences, and life after school.
Mentorship Programs: Alumni mentor current students on university applications, career planning, or skill development.
Alumni Newsletter: A quarterly newsletter about alumni achievements, school updates, and upcoming events.
Social Media: Active LinkedIn, Instagram, and Facebook groups for alumni to stay connected.

content.text: Fundraising and Philanthropy:

steps: Alumni are invited to contribute to school projects (e.g., library renovations, scholarship funds, technology upgrades).
Ethical Guidelines: Donations are voluntary and transparent. Alumni contributions do not influence admissions decisions for their children.

content.text: Post-Secondary Outcomes Tracking:

steps: Survey alumni 1 year and 3 years after graduation to track university enrollment, degree completion, and career placement.
The data guides college counseling, curriculum changes, and school marketing.

content.text: (See the Teacher Guidebook for the detailed alumni coordinator role description.)
Designated Spokesperson:
content.title: 16.9.4 Media and Public Relations

steps: Principal: Main spokesperson for all media inquiries.
Foundation Representative: Handles inquiries about Yayasan governance, major announcements, or sensitive issues.
Subject Matter Experts: The Principal may delegate interviews to teachers or coordinators with prior approval.

content.text: Media Inquiry Protocol:

steps: The media contacts the school reception or the general email address.
Receptionist forwards inquiry to Principal.
The Principal reviews the request and decides to respond, decline, or delegate.
If approved, the Principal or a designee prepares talking points and gives the interview.
After the interview, a summary is filed and shared with the leadership team if significant.

content.text:
Social Media Policy:

Official School Accounts (Managed by approved staff):

steps: Platforms: Instagram, Facebook, YouTube (if applicable).
Content: School events, student achievements, parent information (policy updates, event reminders, academic highlights).
Posting Guidelines: Use a positive, professional tone. Student photos require parent consent (see below).
Moderation: Comments are monitored. Inappropriate content is removed quickly.

content.text: Staff Personal Accounts:

steps: Staff keep their personal and professional social media accounts clearly separate.
Staff must not "friend" current students on personal social media platforms.
Avoid posting content that could reflect badly on the school (e.g., complaints, inappropriate photos, political statements). (See Section 12: Staff Code of Conduct.)

content.text: Student Image Consent:

steps: Parents receive annual photo/video consent forms at the start of the school year (opt-in).
Students without consent are not identifiable in public-facing materials. Their names are left out, and their faces are blurred or left out of photos.
Consent is recorded in student records. (See Section 14: Data Protection for privacy protocols.)

content.text: Celebrating Success: Actively share good news with the community:

steps: Cambridge exam results: Publish overall results and individual high achievers (with student/parent permission).
Olympiad wins, university acceptances, community service impact: Highlight student achievements in newsletters, social media, and press releases.
Media releases: Write press releases for major achievements. Send them to local newspapers and online education platforms.
School website: A "News" section, updated regularly, with stories, photos, and videos.

content.text: Crisis Communications: (See Section 15.2.5 for detailed crisis communication protocols.)

Eduversal Partner Schools keep full records of their parent, student, and community engagement work. These records show that the school meets accreditation standards. They also guide continuous improvement. The table below lists the key evidence and artifacts to keep:

Organization:
content.title: 16.10.1 Key Evidence and Artifacts

steps: Digital Repository: Shared drive with folder structure organized by subsection (16.2 Communications, 16.3 Parent Education, 16.4 Volunteerism, etc.).
Physical Files: Binders in the administrative office, clearly labeled and accessible.
Access: Principal, Assistant Principals, and Accreditation Coordinator have access.

content.text: CIS Standards:
content.title: 16.10.2 Compliance Alignment

steps: Community and Home Partnerships: All elements of Section 16 show real, two-way engagement between the school and families.
Student Wellbeing: Student voice mechanisms, service learning, and safeguarding protocols support students' all-round development. (See Section 9: Safeguarding and Wellbeing.)
Communication: Clear, accessible, bilingual communication builds transparency and trust.

content.text: WASC Categories:

steps: Category A (Organization for Student Learning): Communication structures, stakeholder involvement in the School Improvement Plan (SIP), and clear governance. (See Section 4: Strategic Planning.)

Category C (Support for Student Personal and Academic Growth): Inclusive engagement practices, student leadership opportunities, and parent partnerships build a positive, collaborative school culture.

content.text: Indonesian Regulations:

steps: Public Information Duties: Schools give open information about operations, policies, and student outcomes.
Community Liaison: Yayasan oversight and community partnerships meet regulatory expectations for school-community collaboration.
Parent Rights: Complaints procedures and feedback channels give parents ways to raise concerns and seek resolution.

content.text: Cambridge Centre Requirements:

steps: Candidate and Parent Communications: Exam schedules, results release protocols, and access to secure exam information. (See Section 10: Cambridge Examinations Management.)
Secure Communications: Confidentiality in exam-related communications with students and parents.

content.title: Evidence and artifacts to maintain
rows: Annual communications plan; sample newsletters; parent email templates
PTC schedules and attendance records; PTC summary forms
Annual parent survey results with analysis; complaint logs and resolutions
Workshop agendas, materials, attendance sheets, post-event feedback
Partnership MOUs; annual partnership review reports
Service project plans, photos, student reflections, hours logs
Student survey results; Student Council minutes; focus group notes
Alumni database; event reports; post-secondary outcomes data
Media releases; social media analytics; publication clippings

content.text:
The following annual cycle gives a clear timeline for engagement activities. It helps all Eduversal Partner Schools work in a consistent way.

Annual Engagement Cycle:

Role Clarity:

content.title: Annual Engagement Cycle
rows: PTA elections; Parent Handbook distributed; Welcome Back Assembly
Home visits begin; Parent Workshop #1 (Understanding Cambridge); Student Council elections
Parent Workshop #2 (Supporting EAL Learners); Semester 1 Mid-Term Progress Reports issued (Grades 7–12)
Parent Workshop #3 (Exam Preparation); Holiday celebrations (cultural inclusivity)
Parent Workshop #4 (Digital Citizenship and Online Safety)
Community Partnership Review; Service Learning Showcase
Annual Parent Survey launched; Student Voice Survey #2
Volunteer Appreciation Event; Parent Survey results analysis; Annual Report to Community published
Action planning based on feedback (informs next year's SIP); Staff PD on engagement strategies

content.text: Parent-Teacher Conferences and Student-Led Conferences are not tied to fixed months in this cycle. For Grades 7–12, they follow the semester schedule in Section 6.10 and 16.7.1. Conferences are normally held around the Mid-Term Progress Reports (October and March) and the end-of-semester reports (December and May). The portfolio-led Student-Led Conference is normally held in the December and May windows. Each school sets the dates.

steps: Principal: Overall accountability; strategic direction; high-level communications; crisis management; media spokesperson.
Parent Liaison Coordinator: Day-to-day parent communications; volunteer coordination; PTA liaison; feedback processing; workshop logistics.
Teachers: Classroom-level communications; home visits; PTCs; implementation of engagement strategies.
Student Council Advisor: Lead Student Council meetings; support student voice projects; coordinate student-led events.
Alumni Coordinator: Maintain alumni database; organize alumni events; track post-secondary outcomes. (Role may be combined with Parent Liaison in smaller schools.)

editorialNotes.title: Note on this table
editorialNotes.text: April and May are separate rows in the source that share a cell border (rendering artifact); they are transcribed as two distinct rows with their own activity and owner. The table names only generic role titles, no individuals.

content.text: Eduversal Partner Schools are committed to continuous improvement based on stakeholder feedback and changing best practice. Review Cycle:
content.title: Annual Policy Review Process

steps: Data Collection (May-June): Collect feedback from parents (surveys), teachers (reflection forms), students (voice surveys), and the PTA (exit interviews with outgoing members).
Analysis (June-July): The leadership team reviews trends, finds strengths, and identifies areas that need improvement.
Revision (July-August): Update Section 16 policies, communications plan, workshop calendar, and engagement strategies based on findings.
Approval (August): The Principal approves the revised policies. The Yayasan reviews them for any major changes.
Communication (August): The updated Section 16 is published. Key changes are shared in the Parent Handbook, on the website, and in the August newsletter.

content.text: The following metrics measure how well the engagement work is going:
content.title: Indicators of Success

steps: Parent Survey Response Rate: Target of at least 60%; satisfaction scores rising year-over-year.
PTC Attendance: Target of at least 90% of families taking part.
Volunteer Participation: Growth in the number of parent volunteers, tracked annually.
Student Voice Responsiveness: Evidence that student suggestions were acted on and documented (e.g., new clubs added, policy changes, facility improvements).
Community Partnerships: Lasting relationships that benefit both sides, shown by MOU renewals and partnership impact data.
Service Learning Impact: Number of hours logged, projects completed, and community beneficiaries served.

content.title: Common Challenges and Solutions

content.text: Section 16 connects with several sections of the Principal's Handbook. For full guidance, see:

steps: Section 1: Front Matter and Governance Charter (Yayasan, Foundation Representative roles)
Section 4: Strategic Planning and School Improvement (stakeholder involvement in SIP)
Section 6: Assessment, Reporting, and Data Use (report card formats, progress reporting)
Section 5: Curriculum Architecture (Cambridge curriculum overview)
Section 8: Inclusion, EAL, and Learning Support (support for diverse learners)
Section 9: Safeguarding, Child Protection, and Wellbeing (student wellbeing programs, safer recruitment)
Section 10: Cambridge Examinations Management (exam schedules, results communication)
Section 11: Admissions, Enrollment, and Marketing Ethics (transparent admissions practices)
Section 12: Staff Lifecycle (Staff Code of Conduct, social media policy)
Section 13: Operations, Finance, and Resources (financial transparency, budget reporting)
Section 14: Data Protection, Records, and Information Systems (student image consent, data privacy)
Section 15: Risk Management, Emergency Preparedness, and Business Continuity (emergency communications)

content.title: Common challenges and solutions
rows: Low parent engagement in specific groups
Targeted multilingual outreach; flexible meeting times (evenings, weekends); home visits; culturally responsive engagement; practical support such as childcare or meals
Expand translation services; increase visual communications (infographics, videos); bilingual parent ambassadors to support families who do not speak English
Offer paper alternatives for communications and surveys; SMS communications; school-based information sessions; printed newsletters
Micro-volunteering options (short, one-time tasks); remote volunteering; clearer communication of volunteer impact; recognition events
Build relationships through consistent, transparent communication; listen actively to concerns; close feedback loops visibly; celebrate successes together
